analysis.one_liner: Caps speculative oil futures trading so commercial hedgers keep at least half the market.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and it died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal regulator of futures markets, to write rules capping how much of the oil futures market can be held by financial traders rather than businesses that actually use oil. The rules would guarantee that traditional commercial hedgers — companies that buy or sell oil as part of their real business — collectively hold at least half the positions in petroleum contracts each month. The stated aim was to limit excessive speculation in petroleum markets. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers facing gasoline, diesel, and heating prices that critics link in part to speculative financial trading; commercial oil hedgers like airlines and fuel buyers who compete for positions with financial traders; and the CFTC, which would gain a clear statutory mandate to write the limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers paying energy prices; commercial oil hedgers

how_it_helps.text: It directs the CFTC to set limits on the aggregate positions financial traders can hold in petroleum and related contracts across each month, rather than leaving those positions unlimited.

It requires that traditional bona fide hedgers — businesses with real oil exposure — collectively hold at least 50% of both the long and the short positions in the market, guaranteeing them room to hedge.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms and speculators that hold large petroleum futures positions as an investment rather than a hedge would face binding caps on how much they can hold. If the limits reduced market liquidity, hedging costs for some commercial firms could rise slightly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large financial speculators in oil markets

drawbacks.text: The 50% hedger share is a fixed statutory quota rather than a limit calibrated to market conditions, and many economists dispute how much, if any, commodity speculation actually drives consumer prices — so the rules could restrict trading, reduce liquidity, and raise hedging costs without clearly lowering prices at the pump.
The mandate reaches only petroleum and related products, not the full range of commodities, and its effectiveness would depend entirely on regulations the CFTC chose to write.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real public grievance — the suspicion that financial speculation pushes up gasoline prices — but its core tool, a fixed 50% quota for commercial hedgers, is a blunt instrument whose benefits are uncertain and whose costs fall on market liquidity and trading firms. It was a modest, targeted measure rather than sweeping reform, and its fate matters mainly as an example of how little traction even a single-sponsor idea gets without broader backing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2012, sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, drew no cosponsors, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2013 without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Pryor, a Democrat from Arkansas, introduced the bill on March 27, 2012.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which was its last action.
No senator joined as a cosponsor.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms and speculators holding large petroleum futures positions are better off: the position limits were never enacted, and the parallel CFTC rulemaking on position limits remained contested in court. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death, but nothing was lost beyond a low-cost experiment in tighter limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil-market speculators and trading firms

for.name: Sen. Mark Pryor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought referral to the Senate Agriculture Committee; no other senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 27, 2012 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: United States Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill on the floor; it expired with the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator beyond the sponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested.

industries.industry: Commodity trading firms and financial speculators
industries.note: The bill would cap the aggregate positions these firms can hold in petroleum futures, directly limiting a source of trading revenue. Their gain from the bill's failure was the absence of binding limits in statute.

industries.industry: Commercial oil hedgers (producers, refiners, airlines, fuel buyers)
industries.note: The bill guarantees traditional hedgers at least half of both long and short positions, protecting their access to the market against financial traders. Businesses and consumers both benefit if speculation-driven price swings are curbed.
Producers would gain hedging protections and possibly a calmer price environment, but they would also face new aggregate position limits that did not previously exist in statute.
